title: PAX Good Behavior Game School-Wide Implementation
source_title: Kramer Elementary | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content: Dear Kramer Elementary Families,We are excited to announce that our entire school is partnering this year to implement a powerful, evidence-based strategy called the PAX Good Behavior Game (PAX GBG).What is the PAX Game?The PAX Game is not a separate curriculum or a set of strict rules. Instead, it is a set of strategies used by all teachers and staff throughout the school day to help students build self-regulation, focus, and teamwork."PAX" is a Latin word meaning peace, productivity, health, and happiness. By using PAX school-wide, we create a unified, positive environment in our hallways, cafeteria, playground, and classrooms.Key Terms Your Child Will UsePAX Behaviors: The positive actions, cooperation, and focus we want to see more of at Kramer Elementary.SPLEEMS: Minor disruptions, distractions, or behaviors that get in the way of learning and harmony. We work together to notice and reduce these.PAX Quiet: A quick, gentle signal (using a harmonica and a hand signal) used by staff to gather students' attention instantly and calmly.Tootles: The opposite of "tattling." Students write these small notes to recognize and appreciate kind or helpful acts by their peers.PAX Prizes: Fun, 30-second activity breaks (like "Granny's Wacky Prizes") that classrooms earn for working together to keep SPLEEMS low.Bringing PAX HomeBecause PAX is a school-wide effort, you can easily use these same concepts at home! You can support your student by asking them:"What did PAX look like in the cafeteria or on the playground today?""Did anyone write a Tootle for you, or did you write one for a classmate?""What kind of PAX choices can we make while we get ready for bed tonight?"Thank you for partnering with us to make Kramer Elementary School a peaceful, productive, and joyful place for every student to learn and grow.Warmly,Mrs. Ashley Tebbe, PrincipalKramer Elementary School

summary: Kramer Elementary School is implementing the **PAX Good Behavior Game (PAX GBG)** school-wide, an evidence-based strategy to help students build self-regulation, focus, and teamwork. Key terms students will use include **PAX Behaviors** (positive actions), **SPLEEMS** (minor disruptions to reduce), **PAX Quiet** (attention signal using harmonica), **Tootles** (notes recognizing kind acts), and **PAX Prizes** (30-second activity breaks earned by reducing SPLEEMS). Families can support PAX at home by asking children about their PAX experiences and choices throughout the day.

title: Understanding Bullying vs. Peer Conflict
source_title: Kramer Elementary | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
Counselor 

Corner  Counselor Corner

Bullying vs. Peer Conflict BullyingBullying is unwanted, aggressive behavior among school aged children that involves a real or perceived power imbalance. The behavior is repeated, or has the potential to be repeated, over time. Both kids who are bullied and who bully others may have serious, lasting problems.In order to be considered bullying, the behavior must be aggressive and include:An Imbalance of Power: Kids who bully use their power—such as physical strength, access to embarrassing information, or popularity—to control or harm others. Power imbalances can change over time and in different situations, even if they involve the same people.Repetition: Bullying behaviors happen more than once or have the potential to happen more than once.Bullying includes actions such as making threats, spreading rumors, attacking someone physically or verbally, and excluding someone from a group on purpose.Peer ConflictIt is not bullying when two kids with no perceived power imbalance fight, have an argument, or disagree. These behaviors can occur at different ages, including early childhood, adolescence, and young adulthood. Parents and caregivers, school staff, and other adults can help younger children develop skills for getting along with others in age-appropriate ways. Conflict resolution or peer mediation may be appropriate when these situations occur during adolescence and young adulthood.

summary: **Bullying** is unwanted, aggressive behavior involving a **power imbalance** and **repetition** (or potential for repetition). It includes making threats, spreading rumors, physical or verbal attacks, and intentional exclusion. **Peer conflict** is different—when two kids with no power imbalance fight, argue, or disagree, it's not bullying. Conflict resolution or peer mediation can help address peer conflicts appropriately.

title: PAX Good Behavior Game Classroom Strategies
source_title: Kramer Elementary | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
PAX 

Good 

Behavior 

Game PAX Good Behavior Game

Dear Parents and Caregivers, Your child will be learning in a PAX classroom this year! PAX is a set of evidence-based classroom strategies that help children practice self-regulation, cooperation, positive communication, and focused learning. In a PAX classroom, students and teachers work together to create a safe, caring, and productive learning environment.PAX strategies are used during regular classroom instruction and increase meaningful learning time. PAX Good Behavior Game (GBG) is one of the most effective classroom preventive interventions, improving outcomes for students and teachers while also benefiting families and communities.Below is a list of PAX strategies your child may use in the classroom and throughout the school. We encourage you to ask your child about these strategies and how they help make their classroom a more peaceful, productive, healthy, and happy place to learn. Thank you for partnering with us to support your child’s learning and growth!Pax Vision What is it?-PAX Vision us used to set clear, shared expectations for what we want more of (called PAX) and less of (Spleems) during an activity. Spleem is a made-up word that refers to disruptions or off-task behaviors. Ask Your Child- What were the things everyone wanted more of in the PAX Vision? What were some things everyone wanted less of in the PAX Vision?Wacky PrizesWhat is it?-Wacky Prizes are quick, active, fun rewards for a job well done.Ask Your Child- What Wacky Prize did you get today? What is your favorite Wacky Prize?Beat the TimerWhat is it?-Beat the TImer is a strategy used to help students complete tasks quickly, efficiently, and safely.Ask Your Child- When did you get to play Beat the Timer today? When do you think we could play Beat the Timer at home?PAX StixWhat is it?-PAX Stix is a strategy to increase fairness, attention, an participation. Ask Your Child- When did your teacher use PAX stix today? How did it go? If you get called on and need help, who do you think you will ask?Tootle NotesWhat is it?-Tootle Notes are a strategy used to help children learn to recognize the good and improvement in one another. Ask Your Child- Who did you write a Tootle Note to and what for? Who do you think we could write a Tootle Note for together?Pax OK/Not OKWhat is it?-PAX OK/Not OK is a strategy used to deliver non-verbal feedback to students.Ask Your Child- What kinds of things make your teacher tap on “OK”? What kinds of things need fixed?PAX Good Behavior GameWhat is it?-PAX GBG is a classroom strategy to help young people increase self-regulation, cooperation, and resilience. Teams work together to reduce disruptions and increase prosocial behaviors.Ask Your Child- Do you notice the Spleems decreasing and PAX increasing? How do teammates help each other to be successful?

summary: Students will be learning in a **PAX classroom** this year, using evidence-based strategies to practice self-regulation, cooperation, and focused learning. PAX strategies include **PAX Vision** (setting clear expectations), **Wacky Prizes** (fun rewards), **Beat the Timer** (task completion), **PAX Stix** (fair participation), **Tootle Notes** (recognizing others' good behavior), **PAX OK/Not OK** (non-verbal feedback), and the **PAX Good Behavior Game** (team-based self-regulation). Parents are encouraged to ask their children about these strategies to support learning at home.

source_title: Kramer Elementary | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
Important 

District 

Information Important District Information

Changes to the K-5 Grading System at Talawanda  NEW for the 2026-2027 School Year Grades 3-5 - Moving to a Traditional Letter Grading System (A-F)We are excited to shift our grades 3–5 to a traditional letter grade system (A-F) to provide a more detailed look at your child's overall performance and academic habits. This change aligns our 3rd-5th graders with the expectations they will meet in middle and high school, fostering greater accountability and preparing them for future success.For families, this transition offers a familiar and intuitive way to track progress. While the numerical scale focused on specific milestones, letter grades allow for a wider range of feedback to distinguish between meeting basic requirements and consistently exceeding them. This system ensures a clearer dialogue between teachers and parents, highlighting exactly where a student excels or may need extra support.Here is the breakdown of the traditional letter grading system:A - 90-100%B - 80-89%C - 70-79%D - 60-69%F - 0-59%Grades K-2 - Remaining with the Numerical Grading System (1-4)Grades K–2 will continue using the numerical (1–4) grading system to best support our youngest learners. At this foundational level, education is focused on the progressive development of core skills and meeting specific developmental milestones rather than a cumulative letter grade. The 1–4 scale provides a precise way for teachers to communicate exactly where a student is in their learning journey—from beginning to explore a concept to achieving mastery—ensuring that families have a clear understanding of their child's growth in these critical early years. As a reminder, here is a breakdown of the numerical scores:4 - Consistently/Independently Meeting the Standard3 - Meeting the Standard2 - Approaching the Standard1- Not Yet Meeting the Standard

TSD Title I-A Parent and Family Engagement Policy We invite and encourage our families to review the TSD Title I-A Parent and Family Engagement Policy linked to our website. If you have feedback to share, please contact your student’s Title Reading teacher. There will also be a feedback session on 11/19/26 ahead of the School Board Meeting at the THS Performing Art Center.

TSD One Plan Family Engagement We invite and encourage our families to review the TSD One Plan linked to our website. Talawanda is in year one of our current One Plan. Additional information about the One Plan can be found on the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, linked here.If you have feedback to share or would like to be part of the parent/community advisory group for our One Plan, please contact Ms. Stephanie Aerni, Director of Teaching & Learning (AerniS@talawanda.org). There will also be a feedback session on 11/19/26 ahead of the School Board Meeting at the THS Performing Art Center.

Families are invited to review the **TSD Title I-A Parent and Family Engagement Policy** and the **TSD One Plan** on the district website. A **feedback session for both policies** will be held on **11/19/26** ahead of the School Board Meeting at the THS Performing Art Center. To join the parent/community advisory group or provide feedback, contact Ms. Stephanie Aerni (AerniS@talawanda.org) or your student's Title Reading teacher.
